clue.text: An old copper isn't a handy item

explanation.surface: A collector notes that an old penny is not much use to anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the answer as two words: a thing that is far off is not to hand. A farthing was an old British copper coin worth a quarter of a penny.
explanation.definitionFit: The coin was a quarter-penny piece minted in copper; split in two, the word describes an object a long way off, the opposite of handy.

clue.text: Sacked a politician as underground risk

parts.note: to be fired is to be dismissed from a job
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician is dismissed over a mining hazard.
explanation.walkthrough: Firedamp is the explosive methane gas found in coal mines.
explanation.definitionFit: Explosive methane in coal mines was a deadly hazard to miners below ground.

clue.text: They chew things over to break down spirit in workers

definitions.text: They chew things over to break down

parts.note: rum is a spirit distilled from sugar cane
taken as written
worker ants are a crossword staple for workers

explanation.surface: Union members discuss how to dampen morale among the staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They chew things over' suggests people deliberating, but it means cud-chewing animals such as cows, which chew food again to digest it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle, sheep and goats regurgitate and rechew cud so their food can be digested.

clue.text: Therefore scram!

explanation.surface: A logical conclusion, delivered as an order to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means 'for this reason', and in old usage it is a command to go away from here.

clue.text: Medicine for Mussolini's mare

explanation.surface: A remedy for the dictator's female horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mare' is not a horse but Latin for sea: Mussolini called the Mediterranean 'mare nostrum', 'our sea', the old Roman name.
explanation.definitionFit: A quack remedy is a patent medicine; Mussolini revived the Roman phrase calling the Mediterranean 'our sea'.

clue.text: Result of flak

parts.note: read literally, an aircraft hit by anti-aircraft fire ends up riddled with holes; read as one word, an outcome

explanation.surface: Someone asks what came of all the criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: Flak is anti-aircraft fire, and a plane it hits is 'shot up'; join the words and you have the ordinary word for an outcome.
explanation.definitionFit: An upshot is a final outcome, while a plane damaged by anti-aircraft fire has been shot up.

clue.text: Fixes food to suit pattern

parts.note: pins fix things in place
tripe is cow's stomach eaten as food

explanation.surface: Someone attaches food to their outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin parallel lines on dark cloth are the classic design of a businessman's suit.

clue.text: Jute — as not all authors agree

indicators.note: only part of the words authors agree is used, so a run of their letters is taken

explanation.surface: A remark that historians dispute the story of a Jute.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface seems to say writers dispute some fact about a Jute; 'not all' takes letters from 'authors agree'. Legend makes Horsa and his brother Hengist the Jutish leaders who came to Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend makes him a fifth-century Jutish chief, brother of Hengist, who led the invasion of Kent.

clue.text: Suitable West End mourning wear ? Surely not

definitions.text: Suitable West End mourning wear ? Surely not

parts.words: Suitable West End mourning wear ? Surely not
parts.note: country suits of rough woollen cloth can be made into suits, but they are not worn in smart town for mourning

explanation.surface: A doubtful query about what to wear to a funeral in central London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suitable' means able to be made into suits; rough country cloth suits are the last thing for a sombre occasion in London's fashionable West End.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough woollen country cloth and the suits made from it go by this name.

clue.text: Maxims for our times

parts.note: AD, anno domini, is the era we live in
ages are periods of time

explanation.surface: A remark that wise sayings suit the present day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our' gives AD, the Christian era of our dates; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Old proverbs and sayings are wise maxims.

clue.text: Having undergone normal type conversion ?

parts.note: plain upright printing type is called roman, so text converted into it has been altered in that way; also a person converted to the Church of Rome

explanation.surface: A printer describes text that has been reset in a standard face.
explanation.walkthrough: Upright print is 'roman' type; the word also means converted to Roman Catholicism, so 'conversion' does double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Text set in upright roman print has been so treated, and a convert to Catholicism has also been brought into the Roman fold.

clue.text: It conveys a sense of cool courage

explanation.surface: Something that carries feeling is described as calm bravery.
explanation.definitionFit: Fibres in the body carry sensory signals to the brain; the same word means steady boldness, as in 'hold your nerve'.

clue.text: Poet is soundly swindled

indicators.note: the clue says the word is to be judged by how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: to be done is to be cheated or conned

explanation.surface: A poet is said to have been thoroughly cheated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soundly' looks like 'thoroughly' but signals a homophone. John Donne was the English metaphysical poet.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne was a seventeenth-century English poet, famous for his metaphysical verse.

clue.text: The drive of the Britisher

parts.note: British cars have the steering wheel on the side away from the kerb, because Britons keep to the left of the road

explanation.surface: A remark about what motivates a British person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' suggests ambition, but it is the car's steering arrangement: British vehicles have the wheel on the right because traffic keeps left.
explanation.definitionFit: Cars built for British roads have the steering wheel on the right side, a so-called right-hand drive.

clue.text: For thirty seconds one has quiet at least

parts.note: half a minute, so half the word minute, its first three letters
I is the Roman numeral for one
mum means silent, as in 'keep mum'

explanation.surface: For half a minute, someone keeps silent, at the very least.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thirty seconds' is half a minute, taken as half the word MINUTE. 'Has' joins the next two pieces. The definition reads 'at the least'.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest acceptable amount is what one must have at least, as in 'a bare minimum'.

clue.text: Island birds with anthropomorphic roots

parts.note: the Isle of Man is a crossword's usual island
drakes are male ducks

explanation.surface: Seabirds from an island described by their human-like origins.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the plants: mandrake roots are forked and look like a human figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The plants have forked roots shaped like a human body, the source of much legend.

clue.text: A piper's accidents ?

parts.note: a pipe smoker lights up with thin tapers of wood or paper, and the same word means tumbles or mishaps

explanation.surface: A bagpiper's mishaps on parade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piper' is not a bagpiper but a pipe smoker, whose lighting tapers share a name with falls or mishaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin wood or paper tapers for lighting pipes bear this name, as do falls and mishaps.

clue.text: One may be prone to take things so

definitions.text: One may be prone to take things so

parts.words: One may be prone to take things so
parts.note: 'prone' means flat on one's front, and to accept things without protest is idiomatically to take them flat

explanation.surface: A remark about a person inclined to accept things passively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prone' looks like 'inclined to' but also means lying flat; to take something 'lying down' is to accept it meekly.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying flat is a prone position, and accepting insult without resistance is taking it so.

clue.text: Make a recovery and the game won't be lost

definitions.text: Make a recovery and the game won't be lost

parts.words: Make a recovery and the game won't be lost
parts.note: a gun dog fetches shot birds so none goes missing, and 'game' here means birds killed by hunters

explanation.surface: A sporting comment that a comeback will save the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' is not a match but shot birds, which a gun dog fetches back.
explanation.definitionFit: To get back or fetch something is to recover it, as a gun dog brings back shot birds.

clue.text: Interesting practice, given frequent Rialto rating

definitions.text: Interesting practice, given frequent Rialto rating

parts.words: Interesting practice, given frequent Rialto rating
parts.note: the word means both interest charged on loans and established custom; Shakespeare's Shylock complains that he was berated on the Rialto for taking it

explanation.surface: A remark about a curious custom of scolding often heard in Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interesting practice' is the practice of charging interest. In The Merchant of Venice Shylock says Antonio has often rated (scolded) him on the Rialto about his 'usances'.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word means usury or interest on money and also custom or usage, the sense Shylock uses in Shakespeare.

clue.text: They happen to find an opening in two quarters

indicators.note: the opening sits inside the two compass points

parts.note: E and S, east and south, are two quarters of the compass
E and S, east and south, are two quarters of the compass
a vent is an opening for air or gas

explanation.surface: Something that occurs when a gap is found in two districts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts VENT between E and S, two compass quarters.
explanation.definitionFit: Occurrences are things that take place, so these happenings are what 'they happen' describes.

clue.text: Top engineer needs implement to make a crack

parts.note: CRE stands for Commander Royal Engineers, the senior engineer officer in a British army formation
a vice is a clamping tool on a workbench

explanation.surface: A senior engineer needs a tool to make a fissure.
explanation.walkthrough: CRE (Commander, Royal Engineers) is a military title, the top engineer in a British army division.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow opening or fissure in rock or a wall is a synonym for a crack.

clue.text: Big bottles among Bizet's juvenilia ?

parts.note: Bizet's best-known opera is Carmen; a boyhood version would swap the men for boys

explanation.surface: Large flasks found among the composer's early works.
explanation.walkthrough: Bizet wrote Carmen; as a juvenile work it would be 'Car-boys', which are large wicker-covered bottles.
explanation.definitionFit: Large glass bottles in protective wicker or crates are used for acids and other liquids.

clue.text: Watch Nimrod !

explanation.surface: An order to look at a famous biblical figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' is not a verb but a pocket watch with a hinged lid; Nimrod is the 'mighty hunter' of Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: A pocket watch with a protective lid has this name, and Nimrod is called the mighty one in Genesis.

clue.text: Make insufficient use of briefs, for instance ?

explanation.surface: Someone complains about not wearing short knickers enough.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition splits the answer into two words: to wear too little.
explanation.definitionFit: To under-wear something is to use it too little; briefs are an example of the garments worn beneath clothes.

clue.text: A man needs this tropical kit to get a baboon

definitions.text: A man needs this tropical kit to get a baboon

parts.words: A man needs this tropical kit to get a baboon
parts.note: the missing word is a hard-wearing cotton cloth for tropical uniforms, and it also names an African monkey; put after 'man' it forms the name of a larger baboon

explanation.surface: An explorer needs tropical clothing to hunt a monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is twill cotton used for tropical kit and also a West African baboon; MAN plus it gives MANDRILL, another baboon.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard cotton twill made tropical uniforms, and the same name is borne by a West African baboon related to the mandrill.

clue.text: Its north wall elevation is to scale

definitions.text: Its north wall elevation is to scale

parts.words: Its north wall elevation is to scale
parts.note: 'elevation' and 'scale' sound like architectural drawing terms, but the subject is a Swiss peak whose sheer north face climbers set out to scale

explanation.surface: An architect notes that the drawing of a building's north wall is to scale.
explanation.walkthrough: Drawing terms disguise a mountain: the Swiss Alpine peak whose north face (Nordwand) is a famous climb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bernese Alpine peak is famed for the north face that mountaineers attempt to climb.

clue.text: What might there be to put you out?

definitions.text: What might there be to put you out?

indicators.note: the letters could become something else, so the word there is rearranged
the letters could become something else, so the word there is rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks what could be used to knock you unconscious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might be' rearranges THERE; the whole clue then describes an old anaesthetic.
explanation.definitionFit: This volatile liquid was an early anaesthetic used to render patients unconscious.

clue.text: Magician's spell ?

parts.note: a conjuror performs illusions, and a sailor's stint at the helm is also called by the same word

explanation.surface: An incantation cast by a conjuror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell' is not an incantation but a period of duty, as a sailor's turn at the wheel; it is also what a conjuror performs.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjuror's illusion is this, and so is a sailor's stint of duty at the helm.

clue.text: Saw feature some might describe as tasteful

parts.note: a saw blade has a row of teeth, each one a tooth
taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark about a feature some people find attractive.
explanation.definitionFit: Something delicious or appetising is pleasant to the taste, which is what 'tasteful' means here.

clue.text: " Some act That has no —— of salvation in't " (Hamlet)

definitions.text: Some act That has no —— of salvation in't " (Hamlet

parts.words: Some act That has no —— of salvation in't " (Hamlet
parts.note: the blank in the quotation is the word Shakespeare wrote: Hamlet means to kill Claudius in an act that has no taste of salvation in it

explanation.surface: A quotation from Hamlet with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank: Hamlet, sparing Claudius at prayer, plans to kill him in some act 'That has no relish of salvation in't' (Act 3 Scene 3).
explanation.definitionFit: Here the word means a trace or flavour, the line meaning an act with no taste of salvation in it.

clue.text: Almost all greatness, if misapplied, will make enemies

indicators.note: letters misapplied are put to the wrong use, so they are rearranged
all but the last letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A warning that power abused will turn people against you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost all' drops the last S of GREATNESS, leaving GREATNES; 'if misapplied' rearranges those eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To alienate people is to make enemies of former friends, turning them hostile.
